book_title: Chapter 1: From Chhattisgarh Forest Floors to Global Chocolate Vaults
question: How did a Raipur-based trader of wild forest seeds evolve into a globally audited supplier of Cocoa Butter Equivalents—and what operating cycles tested that transition?

epigraph.quote: The forest gives its harvest once a year; the factory must run every day of the twelve.
epigraph.author: Central Indian Tree-Borne Oilseed Trade Maxim

web_blocks.title: Raipur Roots and the Pivot Out of Commodity Trading (2005–2018)

web_blocks.html: Manorama Industries Limited began on August 9, 2005, in Raipur, Chhattisgarh [8]. Promoters Ashish Saraf, Vinita Saraf, and their associates founded it as a private firm [8]. Chhattisgarh sits at the core of India's central forest belt. That region yields wild tree-borne oilseeds like sal seeds (central Indian sal) and mango kernels [5, 8]. Tribal and forest communities gather these seeds during short seasonal windows across four central Indian states [5, 8]. In its first decade, Manorama worked mainly as a seed trader and basic extractor [8, 12]. It bought raw kernels at harvest and sold crude fats to domestic soap and feed buyers [8, 12].

That legacy trading model earned thin, erratic profits. In FY17, revenue stood at ₹145.48 Cr, which still included trading sales [12]. Yet EBITDA was just ₹3.67 Cr (a 2.5% margin), and net profit was ₹1.38 Cr [12]. Management saw that pure seed trading trapped working capital without pricing power. In FY18, the firm began exiting low-margin trading and shifted toward specialty fats [12]. Revenue rose to ₹219.38 Cr, EBITDA jumped fivefold to ₹18.51 Cr (8.4% margin), and PAT hit ₹10.36 Cr [12]. To capture higher value, Manorama had to turn crude sal, mango, and shea fats into Cocoa Butter Equivalents (CBE) [9, 23]. That shift required an integrated refinery and solvent-fractionation plant [9, 23].

web_blocks.title: The 2018 BSE SME IPO, Birkoni Commissioning & Mainboard Migration

web_blocks.html: In early 2018, the firm became a public limited company [8]. It raised ₹64 Cr in a September 2018 IPO at ₹188 per share (face value ₹10) [9]. Shares listed on the BSE SME board on October 4, 2018, under code 541974 [9]. Management used the IPO cash to build a greenfield plant at Birkoni Industrial Area near Raipur [9, 23]. Whole-Time Director Gautam Pal led plant engineering and operations [24]. Meanwhile, Vinita Saraf and Ashish Saraf led global client approvals, and CFO Ashok Jain arranged bank credit lines [24].

The Birkoni plant went live in March 2020 as COVID-19 lockdowns hit global trade [23]. Even with pandemic delays, the firm completed its two-year SME listing record. In October 2020, the Board approved moving to the BSE Main Board and listing on NSE (Symbol: MANORAMA) [10]. In July 2021, Manorama raised ₹101.68 Cr through a preferential issue of 7,98,180 shares at ₹1,274 each [11]. Funds like White Oak, Ashoka India Equity, and India Acorn bought into the round [11]. Management put ~₹65 Cr into capex and ~₹36.69 Cr into working capital [11].

web_blocks.takeaway: Manorama's evolution was a deliberate, capital-intensive climb from a 2.5% EBITDA-margin forest-seed trader in FY17 to a 26% operating-margin integrated CBE manufacturer by FY26.

web_blocks.html: Manorama's growth has moved in clear cycles rather than a straight line [7, 13]. New plants first absorb cash and raise fixed costs before sales catch up [7, 13]. When Birkoni Phase-1 started in FY20, revenue jumped 83.8% from ₹102.4 Cr (FY19) to ₹188.2 Cr [13]. EBITDA reached ₹43.9 Cr, or a 23.3% margin [13]. Then FY21 and FY22 brought a clear dip. High ocean freight and a weaker product mix cut EBITDA margins to 17.1% in FY21 (₹34.7 Cr on ₹202.6 Cr sales) [13]. In FY22, margins fell further to 13.9% (₹38.9 Cr on ₹279.1 Cr sales) [13].

From FY23 to FY24, Manorama built its next wave of plants. It added a 30,000 TPA refinery and interesterification unit in May 2023 [23]. In April 2024, it added a 25,000 TPA fractionation line [23]. Sales rose to ₹350.8 Cr in FY23 and ₹457.1 Cr in FY24, with EBITDA margins steady near 16.1% (₹56.5 Cr and ₹73.5 Cr) [13]. Yet cash flow fell hard behind the scenes. Ahead of the April 2024 launch, Manorama stocked up on West African shea nuts and Indian kernels [6, 7]. That buildup pushed FY24 operating cash flow (CFO) to -₹153.5 Cr [6, 7]. Total debt to gross cash accruals jumped from 2.52x in FY23 to 6.50x in FY24 [6]. Both CARE Ratings and India Ratings flagged this working-capital strain even as they upgraded Manorama to A+ [6, 7].

The payoff arrived in FY25 and FY26. Two drivers came together: full availability of 40,000–47,500 MTPA fractionation capacity at Birkoni and a global cocoa shortage [1, 2, 5, 25]. High cocoa prices pushed chocolate makers to raise CBE use [25]. Sales surged 68.7% YoY in FY25 to ₹771 Cr, with 24% OPM and ₹110 Cr PAT [1]. In FY26, sales jumped 77.3% YoY to ₹1,367 Cr, with 26% OPM and ₹225 Cr PAT [1]. TTM sales through September 2026 reached ₹1,617 Cr, with PAT at ₹284 Cr [1]. Meanwhile, H2 FY26 inventory sales released cash and lifted FY26 CFO to +₹250 Cr [1]. In June–July 2026, a ₹500 Cr QIP added fresh equity for the next capex cycle [22].

web_blocks.title: THE OPERATING CYCLE PATTERN
paragraphs: Each Manorama expansion follows three clear steps. First, heavy capex and seed stocking depress CFO and lift short-term debt. Second, customer audits take 12 to 24 months to turn into commercial CBE orders. Third, higher plant utilization drives operating leverage and lifts EBITDA margins into the mid-20% range.

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand Manorama Industries without getting dazzled by its recent growth numbers, you and I have to start in the forests of Chhattisgarh, not in a Mumbai brokerage presentation. In August 2005, when Ashish Saraf and Vinita Saraf incorporated Manorama Industries Private Limited in Raipur, the business looked deceptively simple—and dangerously fragile.

Central India's forests produce two extraordinary tree-borne oilseeds: sal seeds from the towering central Indian sal trees and mango kernels discarded by India's massive mango-processing belt. For decades, tribal and forest-dwelling communities across Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, and Madhya Pradesh gathered these seeds during brief, unforgiving harvest windows—sal in the pre-monsoon heat of May and June, mango kernels in the summer, and later shea nuts across the West African savannah between November and February. Back in the mid-2000s, Manorama bought those seeds, traded them, or extracted crude fats for low-margin industrial uses like soap and cattle feed.

You can see the harsh economics of that early model right in the pre-IPO numbers. In FY17, Manorama generated ₹145.48 crore in revenue—yet earned an EBITDA of just ₹3.67 crore and a net profit of ₹1.38 crore. That is a 2.5% operating margin. One bad monsoon, one adverse freight swing, or one delayed receivable could wipe out an entire year's profit. By FY18, as management began exiting low-margin commodity trading, revenue climbed to ₹219.38 crore and EBITDA jumped fivefold to ₹18.51 crore, an 8.4% margin. Management realized that the money was not in gathering seeds; it was in the precision chemistry required to turn wild exotic fats into a drop-in replacement for cocoa butter.

book_subsections.title: Building Birkoni: The Hard Pivot from Trader to Manufacturer
paragraphs: In 2018, Manorama made the defining bet of its corporate life. It converted into a public limited company, launched an IPO in September 2018 at ₹188 per share, and listed on the BSE SME platform on October 4, 2018, raising roughly ₹64 crore. Instead of using that money to pad working capital, management poured it into an integrated manufacturing complex at Birkoni in Mahasamund district, outside Raipur. Whole-Time Director Gautam Pal took charge of building the plant—linking seed milling, solvent extraction, refining, and high-precision fractionation under one roof—while Vinita Saraf and Ashish Saraf worked the phones with European and Japanese chocolate makers, and CFO Ashok Jain arranged working-capital bank lines.

Timing, as it often does in industrial manufacturing, tested their nerve. Birkoni Phase-1 commissioned in March 2020, the exact month global commerce froze under COVID-19 lockdowns. Yet the strategic logic held. By October 2020, after completing the mandatory two years on the SME board, the company approved its migration to the BSE Main Board and NSE. In July 2021, institutional investors—including White Oak India Equity Fund, Ashoka India Equity Investment Trust, and India Acorn Fund—injected ₹101.68 crore via a preferential allotment at ₹1,274 per share. That equity cushion funded a 30,000 TPA refinery and interesterification unit in May 2023 and a transformative 25,000 TPA fractionation line in April 2024.

Think about what that transition meant operationally. Before Birkoni, Manorama was at the mercy of third-party processors and crude-fat traders. With Birkoni running end-to-end—from raw seed cleaning to deodorized specialty butter—Manorama could finally walk into quality-audit rooms in Switzerland, Belgium, and Japan and guarantee batch-to-batch triglyceride consistency.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Notice how Manorama's promoters used equity markets at every inflection point—₹64 crore in the 2018 IPO, ₹101.68 crore in 2021, and ₹500 crore via QIP in mid-2026. In a business where raw material must be bought in bulk months before it is sold, permanent equity is the shock absorber that keeps seasonal working-capital debt from breaking the balance sheet.

book_subsections.title: Reading the Past Operating Cycles Through a Skeptic's Lens
paragraphs: If you look at Manorama's journey from FY19 to FY26, you will notice that the P&L and the cash-flow statement often told two different stories. In FY20, Birkoni's startup pushed revenue up 84% from ₹102.4 crore to ₹188.2 crore with a 23.3% EBITDA margin. Then came a three-year digestion phase: margins compressed to 17.1% in FY21 and 13.9% in FY22 as ocean freight spiked and product mix lagged, before stabilizing near 16.1% in FY23 and FY24.

More importantly, during FY24—right before the big 25,000 TPA fractionation expansion went live in April 2024—Manorama absorbed ₹153.5 crore of negative operating cash flow to stockpile shea nuts and forest kernels. Credit rating agencies flagged the jump in leverage as total debt to gross cash accruals climbed from 2.52x to 6.50x. Only when the new fractionation lines ramped up in FY25 and FY26, aided by a global cocoa butter shortage and a 7,500 MTPA debottlenecking in March 2026, did revenue explode from ₹457.1 crore in FY24 to ₹771 crore in FY25 and ₹1,367 crore in FY26. Operating margins expanded to 26.4%, PAT doubled to ₹225 crore, and FY26 operating cash flow swung back to +₹250 crore.

In June and July 2026, management tapped institutional markets again with a ₹500 crore QIP—using ₹150 crore to pare cash-credit debt and earmarking the rest for a ₹460 crore capex cycle and Burkina Faso backward integration. That tells you the three-act rhythm of Manorama: build capacity and stock seeds, endure a temporary cash-flow trough, and then harvest operating leverage.

book_subsections.title: From Raipur Seed Trader to Mainboard Specialty Formulator
paragraphs: What makes Manorama's corporate arc unusual in Indian agro-processing is that it did not start as a diversified conglomerate chasing a hot trend. Incorporated in 2005 in Raipur, Chhattisgarh, and rooted in decades of family familiarity with central Indian forest produce, the company spent its first decade learning the hardest part of the trade: collecting, cleaning, and crushing wild sal seeds and mango kernels when most organized edible-oil refiners refused to touch them.

The strategic inflection arrived when management realized that crude sal fat and mango butter were merely intermediate inputs. By investing in solvent extraction, physical refining, and precision dry/solvent fractionation at Birkoni, Manorama captured the high-margin downstream step—turning raw forest fats into custom-tailored Cocoa Butter Equivalents that global confectioners previously sourced almost exclusively from European and Malaysian giants. That transition from commodity crusher to specialty ingredient partner is why operating margins structurally re-rated from single digits in the early years to 26.4% in FY26.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Every specialty chemical or food-ingredient compounder looks effortless in hindsight. The real lesson of Chapter 1 is that Manorama's 26% operating margins in FY26 were bought with seven years of heavy capex, 3-to-5-year customer audits, and uncomfortable working-capital troughs in FY20, FY22, and FY24.
